sections.title: On the Use of Holy Names and Sefer Yetzira
sections.html:
The Sages said that one who knows the secret of God's names and of the letters in Sefer Yetzira can create things in the world through holy names and combinations of letters, and it is not forbidden for the righteous to do so (Sanhedrin 67b; SA 179:15). This is because such creation accords with the rules by which the world was created, and involves no turning to forces of impurity that would bypass the ordinary order of God's governance of the world and disrupt it. "Rava said: If the righteous wished, they could create a world." That is, if the righteous were free of sin, they could create a world. But in practice they cannot, as it is stated (Yeshayahu 59:2): "But your iniquities have separated between you and your God" (Sanhedrin 65b). However, they can create various creatures, as is related of Rav Ḥanina and Rav Oshaya, who would sit every Shabbat eve and engage in the laws of Yetzira (formation), and a third-grown calf would be created for them and they would eat it (Sanhedrin 67b). Rashi explained that they did not do so intentionally; rather, because they were engaged in Sefer Yetzira, it was created of its own accord. In any case, they did not do this for personal needs, for it is forbidden to make use of holy names and Sefer Yetzira for one's livelihood or for other personal needs. Similarly, it is related (Sanhedrin 65b) of Rava that he created a golem in the likeness of a man, but his colleague Rabbi Zeira was not pleased with this and returned it to its dust. Apparently, according to the Rambam and those who hold like him (above 19:4), all these accounts of the creation and formation of things are nothing but parables, and not events that really happened.

In practice, the vast majority of the sages of Israel did not try to create or change things with the help of holy names and Sefer Yetzira, for this is not the proper way to cleave to God and to add goodness and blessing to the world. Rather, the straight way that God gave Israel to cleave to Him is through studying Torah and fulfilling the mitzvot. And the more Israel delves into the Torah and its secrets, the better it knows how to fulfil the mitzvot and to add life and blessing to itself and to the world in the most stable, profound and excellent way.1

sections.title: Caution in Using Holy Names and Sefer Yetzira
sections.html:
The Rishonim and Aḥaronim warned that it is permitted to make use of God's names only for the sake of Heaven, and not for any other purpose. And when an additional purpose enters into the mention of the names, there is a prohibition in this. This is the meaning of the Sages' saying (Avot 1:13): "And one who makes use of the crown passes away"; that is, one who makes use of God's names, which are the crown of the Omnipresent, for his own needs passes away from the world (Rema YD 246:21). The Sages further said (Avot De-Rabbi Natan 12:13): "Whoever makes use of the Explicit Name has no share in the World to Come." And so the Sages taught (Kiddushin 71a) to be very careful with the honour of the holy names; for although it is a great virtue to study their meaning, since each name reveals a particular facet of the divine revelation, one must be careful with their honour. Therefore the Sages were accustomed to teach their disciples "the four-letter Name" only once in seven years. It is related that Rava thought to expound the holy Name a little in his public discourse; a certain elder told him that the Name must be concealed and hidden, and he heeded his advice and refrained from expounding it in public. "The Rabbis taught: At first the twelve-letter Name would be transmitted to everyone; once the unruly (those who used it for their own needs) multiplied, it would be transmitted to the modest among the priesthood… Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: The forty-two-letter Name is transmitted only to one who is modest and humble, who has reached the midpoint of his life, who does not get angry, does not get drunk and does not insist on his own way; and whoever knows it, is careful with it and guards it in purity is beloved above and pleasing below, his awe is cast upon people, and he inherits two worlds, this world and the World to Come."

And so Rabbi Yosef Albo explained (Ha-ikkarim 1:18): "For the names are like the tools of the craft of the Omnipresent, for He placed in their power that signs and wonders be performed through them. And one who uses them according to the will of the Omnipresent, like the prophets, or for the honour of the Omnipresent, like the pious, is beloved above and pleasing below, does not die in the midst of his days and does not fall into the hands of his enemies… But one who uses them of his own accord and not for the honour of the Omnipresent is cut off in the midst of his days, falls into the hands of his enemies, and will in the end come to a bad end." Therefore, when wicked people rose up against righteous people to kill them, they were killed and did not try to escape with the help of holy names. For there is no righteous person on earth who is free of all sin, and as long as there is any flaw in him, he may not save himself with holy names; rather, he should try to be saved by all the natural means that God has set before human beings, and whatever God wills will be. And if he tries to save himself by means of a Name, it will not help him. We learn this from what the Sages related (Yevamot 49b) about Yeshayahu the prophet: when the wicked king Menashe sent to kill him, Yeshayahu the prophet uttered a holy Name and was swallowed up inside a cedar tree. The king's messengers began to saw the cedar, and when they reached his mouth his soul departed, for since he had sinned with his mouth by words of accusation against Israel, he could not be saved. It follows that it is not God's will that His Name be used in order to be saved in a way that is not natural.2

sections.title: Refraining from 'Practical Kabbala'
sections.html:
Because of the concern about using holy names without pure intent, even by completely righteous people, the kabbalists and poskim instructed that one refrain from this (Rema YD 246:21; Levush 179:15; Shakh 18). And the holy Arizal said that even at the time when people could purify themselves from impurity with the ashes of the [red] heifer, only a completely righteous person, whom even the accusers love, was permitted to use holy names. And today, when there is no possibility of purification with the ashes of the red heifer, even completely righteous people may not use holy names. In addition, since the righteous refrained from using the names, corruptions crept into the precise form of the names and the procedures for their operation. Therefore one who uses holy names at the present time needs to repent (Sha'ar Ha-mitzvot, Parashat Shemot; Sha'ar Ru'aḥ Ha-kodesh 13b).

And so Rav Eliyahu Guttmacher wrote (Tzafnat Pa'ane'aḥ 9) that it is good to study the meaning of the holy names, as it is stated (Tehillim 91:14): "Because he has desired Me, I will deliver him; I will set him on high, because he has known My name," but it is forbidden to use them for 'practical Kabbala'. Except for those to whom it has become known, "through a revelation of Eliyahu or otherwise through clear signs, that it is the will of God, blessed be He, that they engage in this, and that they came into the world for this purpose, and their souls are suited for it. Only in this way did the Tanna'im and Amora'im make use [of the names], and also afterward in the generations that followed, those who engaged in this." But other sages and righteous people must keep away from engaging in 'practical Kabbala'. And it is not even advisable to study its ways, for in a time of trouble one will find it hard to stop oneself from acting by means of it "after he has already learned."

There is a lower way of changing things in the world through spiritual action, namely by adjuring angels, without using holy names and Sefer Yetzira. This is the way of half-sages, who do not understand the holy names and the secrets of creation, but have learned superficially the last stage of the devolution of life into this world, that is, the names of the angels appointed directly over the particulars of this world. And they try to influence what happens in the world by adjuring the angel appointed over that matter. And although this is a low way that is closer to the ways of sorcery, it is not forbidden as sorcery, since one who does so does not turn to the forces of impurity, but to the spiritual force through which life flows to that creature. This is the main activity of 'practical kabbalists', who indeed do not transgress the prohibition of sorcery, but do transgress the guidance of the rabbis and kabbalists who warned against engaging in 'practical Kabbala', and wrote that one who engages in it renders his soul impure, as will be explained in the next halakha.3

sections.title: The Danger in Using 'Practical Kabbala'
sections.html:
Because of all this, the rabbis and the masters of the hidden wisdom warned those who engage in 'practical Kabbala', whether through holy names or through adjuring angels, that they endanger their souls. For if they use holy names with intent that is not pure, they desecrate the Name and harm themselves in this world and in the World to Come. All the more so when it is almost certain that corruptions have crept into the uses of the names. Even when they try to act in a lower world, by adjuring angels and not with names, and consequently do less damage to the honour of Heaven, since they interfere in God's governance of the world in a way that is not natural, they arouse accusations against themselves. In addition, since their activity is in the 'world of Asiya', which is the lowest of the worlds, the evil in it is more intermingled with the good, and consequently the influence of harmful forces (mazikim) in it is greater. Therefore even when they adjure angels to do good deeds, evil becomes mixed into them and their deeds. And since that evil enters in a way that is not natural, it is hard to contend with it and defend against it; therefore, even if at first they succeed in helping, later on the evil mixed into it will prevail and do more harm (Sha'arei Kedusha part 3, 6).

And so it is written in Sefer Ḥasidim (205): "One who engages in adjurations of angels or of demons… his end will not be good, and he will see evils in his body or in his children all his days. Therefore a person should keep far from doing any of these… for in the end he will have no remedy; how many have done so and how many have inquired, and some of them were impoverished, or converted out of the faith, or fell into a grave illness, or their offspring [did]… And there is nothing good for a person but to pray to the Holy One, blessed be He. And if he sets out on a journey, he should not say an adjuration of angels to guard him on the way, but should pray before the Holy One, blessed be He, for all his needs, for He is merciful and gracious and relents of evil. And how many prophets were killed and did not adjure by the holy Name, but stood in prayer. They said: If He does not hear our prayer, we will know that we are not worthy of being saved. And they would act only through prayer." It further says (972): "The harmful forces provoke only one who provokes them," such as one who engages in adjurations and the like.

After all these things, if there is someone who engages in 'practical Kabbala' and does not suffer afflictions, he is apparently a fraud and his deeds change nothing in the spiritual worlds, and consequently the harmful forces were not aroused against him.4

sections.title: Healing Through Words of Torah
sections.html:
It is forbidden to use verses of the Torah as a segula (a charm-like remedy) for healing, for example saying over a wound or an illness the verse (Shemot 15:26): "All the sickness that I placed upon Egypt I will not place upon you, for I am the Lord who heals you" (Shevuot 15b). For the Torah was given to Israel so that they would study it and fulfil its mitzvot, and not so that they would make it into a tool for segulot. If, in addition, the verse or incantation contained one of God's names, and he spat before saying it, in the manner of whisperers who used to spit before reciting the incantation, his sin is more severe. This is what is called 'one who whispers over a wound', of whom the Sages said that he has no share in the World to Come (Sanhedrin 90a; 101a).

But before the onset of an illness or danger, it is permitted to say verses for protection against them, as the Sages said (Shevuot 15b) that it is permitted to say verses for the sake of protection against harmful forces and mishaps, as many are accustomed to say before going to sleep the psalm (Tehillim 91): "He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High shall abide in the shadow of the Almighty." For in saying the verses before the illness or trouble has come, there is a general prayer to God, in whose hand everything is; but when they are said after the trouble or illness has come, they are used as a charm-like incantation that activates various spiritual forces without turning and praying to God.

The prohibition of healing through words of Torah applies specifically to using certain verses as a charm-like incantation without turning to God in prayer; but it is permitted to say verses as part of a prayer to God that He heal him of the illness or save him from the trouble. And so many are accustomed to say psalms in their time of trouble, for the chapters of Tehillim contain all kinds of prayers and praises to God. And the one praying may choose chapters that express his distress and his personal prayer.

Similarly, the prohibition of healing through words of Torah applies specifically when the words of Torah are used as a segula. But one who studies Torah in order to understand God's word and His guidance, since through his study he connects to the source of life, naturally draws blessing upon himself through it, and he may intend and hope that through the mitzva of Torah study healing or salvation will also be drawn to him. As Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said (Eruvin 54a): "One who is walking on the road and has no escort – let him engage in Torah… If he feels pain in his head – let him engage in Torah… If he feels pain in his throat – let him engage in Torah… If he feels pain in his innards – let him engage in Torah… If he feels pain in his bones – let him engage in Torah… If he feels pain in his whole body – let him engage in Torah, as it is stated (Mishlei 4:22): 'For they are life to those who find them, and healing to all his flesh.'" That is, since one who studies Torah connects to God, the source of life, and engages in His orderly guidance for the world, he is saved through it from dangers and illnesses (Maharal, Maharsha, Torat Ḥayim). Similarly, the Sages said (Rosh Hashana 4a) that a person whose son is ill may give charity so that his son will live; and not only that, but they said he is considered 'completely righteous', for since his intent is to fulfil a mitzva, and even if his son is not healed he will not regret the charity he gave, there is no prohibition in his asking that the merit of the mitzva help heal his son (Rashi there; Ḥadrei De'ah 179:8).5

sections.title: Placing a Book [on the Sick] as a Segula for Healing
sections.html:
Just as it is forbidden to heal oneself with words of Torah, so it is forbidden to place a Torah scroll or tefillin on a child in order to heal him, or to put him to sleep if he suffers from insomnia. For the Torah was given so that people would study it and fulfil its mitzvot, and thereby merit life and blessing, and not so that they would use it as a segula for healing the body (Yerushalmi, Shabbat 6:2; Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 11:12; SA 179:9).

However, in a situation of mortal danger, it is permitted to place a Torah scroll on a sick person. For this reason some were accustomed to place a Torah scroll on a woman having a difficult labour (Be'er Sheva, Sanhedrin 101a). And some say that this involves disrespect for the honour of the Torah scroll; rather, they should place the scroll at the entrance to the room, and the merit of the Torah will protect her (Ḥinukh Beit Yehuda 71). Today, even bringing a Torah scroll to the entrance of the delivery room is considered not in keeping with the honour of the Torah scroll, and so in practice the use of this segula has lapsed. In addition, since medicine has developed greatly, one should minimise the use of segulot and instead act according to the guidance of the Torah, which taught that one should follow accepted medical instructions, and pray much that God send blessing upon the work of the doctors' hands.

It is a good custom for soldiers to take with them a small book of Tehillim or a small siddur as a segula for protection in battle and in order to pray from it from time to time. And there is no concern in this of the prohibition of using words of Torah as a charm-like incantation, for taking the book is meant to express cleaving to God and to make it possible to pray from it. And even if he does not pray from it, there is no prohibition in this, for we have already learned in the previous halakha that in order to protect against an illness or trouble that has not yet come, it is not forbidden to say a verse; similarly, it is permitted to take a book as a segula to protect against a trouble that has not yet come.

sections.title: Amulets
sections.html:
An amulet (kamei'a) is a natural substance, or a written charm-like incantation, intended to heal or to protect against harmful forces and the evil eye, or for success in one's livelihood or for an easy birth. Some amulets are intended for a particular illness and some for general health. Usually the amulet is placed inside a small bag or a leather pouch that is worn around the neck or attached to another place on the body. Examples of natural substances: special stones; parts of animals, such as a bone, nails, feathers or a fox's tooth; kinds of plants, such as roots or leaves; powder from stones or plants. Very often a piece of parchment or paper on which names and verses are written is placed inside the amulet, each people according to its religion, for the use of amulets is widespread among many peoples. Sometimes the amulet is a ring, a chain or a medallion bearing a form with symbolic meaning, or letters and allusions to names, or parts of a verse.

Those who wear amulets believe that when a person has a problem or weakness in a certain area, if he takes a substance that symbolises the repair of the problem or the completion of what he lacks, the charm-like power in that substance will influence the person to strengthen him, guard him and save him from that problem. Likewise, each letter has its own character, and every combination of letters has a special meaning. And when a person who is in danger or has a problem carries on his body an amulet containing a 'written incantation' (ketav laḥash), with combinations of letters and words directed against that danger or weakness, he can, with the help of the charm-like power in the amulet, be saved from the trouble and overcome the obstacles in his path.

In the distant past, doctors held that amulets could help in healing, and the sages of Israel did not dispute them, and permitted their use on condition that they involved no prohibition. Therefore, if the amulet contains names of idols, it is forbidden to use it because of the prohibition of idolatry; and if the amulet contains names and allusions that sorcerers use, it is forbidden to use it because of the prohibition of sorcery. But when the amulet does not rely on impure forces of idolatry or sorcery, even if it was devised by gentiles and written by gentiles, there is no prohibition in using it (SA 179:12).

However, regarding Shabbat, only if it is a proven amulet (kamei'a mumḥe), that is, one that has already healed three times, is it considered part of a person's attire, and it is permitted to go out with it on Shabbat into the public domain. But if the amulet is not proven, one should not go out with it on Shabbat into the public domain (Shabbat 61a-b).6

sections.title: Amulets with Names and Verses
sections.html:
Many amulets in ancient times were based on a 'written incantation', that is, letters and words alluding to the power required for protection, strengthening or success. As we learned in the previous halakha, when names of idols, or verses from the cultic writings of idolatry, or allusions that sorcerers use were written in amulets, the amulets were forbidden for use because of the prohibition of idolatry or sorcery.

It is also forbidden to write holy names and verses from the Tanakh in an amulet, for it is forbidden to write holy names and verses from the Tanakh outside the framework of a complete book of the Tanakh. Indeed, for a great need of a mitzva, such as for Torah study or writing a prayer book, the Sages permitted writing parts of the Torah and names, but they were not lenient about this for amulets (Responsa Rashba 2:281; SA 179:12). However, in a situation of mortal danger, when those present think that an amulet with holy names or parts of verses can help, it is permitted to write such an amulet and use it in order to heal an illness (Shulḥan Gavoha 179:25).7

Once an amulet containing names or parts of verses has already been written, whether it was written with permission for the sake of saving life or written without permission, it is permitted to use it even not for the sake of saving life. But the permission is only in order to protect against troubles and illnesses so that they do not appear; but for a person who has already become ill, as long as his illness does not involve danger to life, it is forbidden to use an amulet containing verses or names, because it is forbidden to use words of Torah as a segula for healing (Shevuot 15b; SA 179:12; above halakha 5).

In order to avoid a doubtful prohibition, the careful among the writers of amulets made sure not to write parts of verses or names; rather, when they wished to allude to a certain verse, they combined the first letter of each word of that verse. And when they wished to mention certain names, they wrote one letter of each name and wove it in among the letters that alluded to the verses.

sections.title: Those Who Hold That One Should Not Use Amulets
sections.html:
According to the Rambam and his school, amulets are of no use at all, and it is not fitting for the wise to imagine that there is any truth in the words of those who engage in them. Nor should one be impressed by their belief that the amulet must be written in holiness and purity and that through this the amulet will work wonders. "All these things are not fit for a perfect man to hear, all the more so to believe" (Guide of the Perplexed 1:61). However, when many people believed in their power to heal, the Sages permitted using them in order to settle the mind of the sick person (Rambam, Hilkhot Shabbat 19:14; ibid., Hilkhot Avoda Zara 11:11).

Following on from this, many hold that today one should not use amulets, because only in ancient times, when doctors held that amulets could help, did the Sages agree to permit their use for healing and other needs. But now that doctors have stopped believing in amulets, and only various mystics believe that they have a charm-like spiritual ability to heal, one who uses them abandons the way of the Torah and the mitzvot, which bring blessing and protection to Israel, and is dragged after foreign beliefs.

And according to Rabbi Yehuda He-ḥasid and his school, although it is possible that amulets sometimes have a charm-like ability to help, it is right not to use them, because their use causes a person to believe in their charm-like power instead of believing in God and strengthening himself in the Torah and mitzvot, and therefore their harm is greater than their benefit. And so he wrote (Sefer Ḥasidim 1714): "If a sage, whether a gentile or a Jew, says to you, 'I will write you an amulet'" for a bridegroom, or so that your words will be accepted before the ministers, or so that you will become rich – do not take it. For the amulet causes one to trust in those vanities instead of relying on God, and it is stated (Mishlei 3:5): "Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding," and it is stated (Devarim 18:13): "You shall be wholehearted with the Lord your God." Therefore he should trust in the Lord his God and pray only to Him. And if his prayer is not answered, he should know that this is so from God. And if he seeks help in amulets, this is like one who has a master, and when he is not answered by him, instead of thinking that his prayer was not heard because of a sin of his, he goes to another minister to ask him for help, as if his master had no power to help him. He further wrote (section 469) that engaging in writing amulets is dangerous, for the harmful forces strike those who engage with them, "such as one who, he or his forefathers, wrote amulets, or engaged in adjurations or in sorcery… therefore a person should not engage in them." And even for the sake of saving life one should not engage "in adjurations and amulets, for this is not wisdom, for a person shortens his life and the life of his offspring… rather, he should pray to the Holy One, blessed be He, regarding every affliction and illness and every distress and trouble" (he wrote similarly in sections 205; 470).

And some wrote that although precise written incantations can help, in practice great corruptions have crept into the various written incantations, and sometimes names of impurity from the traditions of gentile sorcerers have even entered them. In addition, one may not use holy names for human needs in the manner of 'practical Kabbala' (Ramak in Pardes Rimonim 21:1; the Arizal in Sha'ar Ha-mitzvot, Parashat Shemot; above halakhot 1-4).

sections.title: The Response of Those Who Support Amulets, and the Practical Halakha
sections.html:
Indeed, there were rabbis throughout the Jewish diaspora who were accustomed to use amulets, especially amulets containing holy names and prayers, and they noted that the more the amulet is written in holiness, after fasting and immersion, and the more the one being healed knows the content of the amulet, or at least cleaves to the general idea of trust in God, the more the amulet will help him (Rav Eliyahu Ha-kohen). And they explained that just as God gave permission to go to doctors to be healed, so He consented that the charm-like power in an amulet be used (Rabbi Eliezer Papo). Against the claim that it is forbidden to use 'practical Kabbala', Rabbi Yehuda Fetaya explained that the prohibition is to adjure by the holy names, but it is permitted to write names without adjurations, and the holiness of the names in an amulet written with intent can help protect the bearer of the amulet from harmful forces (Beit Leḥem Yehuda 43b). Against the claim that corruptions have crept into the names and incantations in amulets, Rav Yitzḥak Kaduri replied that this claim is correct regarding unfamiliar names found in various amulets, but not against those who use familiar names and their allusions, such as 'Ana Be-khoaḥ' and the seventy-two names derived from the verses "And [the angel of God] moved… and came… and [Moshe] stretched out" (Shemot 14:19-21). And Rav Eliyahu Guttmacher was careful not to write names, but wove in initials of prayer texts and verses from Tehillim, so that the whole matter of the amulets he wrote was in the nature of continual prayer (Tzafnat Pa'ane'aḥ 9). The writers of amulets further argued that rather than Jews being tempted to go to sorcerers who would give them amulets connected to idolatry and names of impurity, "in order to save Israel from going to the gentiles, as is known," it is right to write amulets for them based on holy names and prayers (Rav Kaduri).8

In summary, since there is no mitzva or recommendation of the sages of the Mishna and Talmud to use an amulet, and in addition, some even opposed its use, it is right not to use amulets. Rather, one should act according to the guidance of the Sages, who instructed a person upon whom sufferings have come to examine his deeds and repent, and to turn to God in prayer that He help him, and by virtue of this God will watch over him to support him in the way that is most right for him. And this is the practice of most of Israel (above, in halakha 6, it is explained that it is permitted to carry Tehillim or a siddur in one's pocket).

And those who wish to use amulets written by God-fearing people have something to rely on, and sometimes, when a person is in a state of anxiety, it may even be proper to encourage him to carry an amulet. And the more the amulet expresses prayer and faith in God, and the bearer of the amulet knows this, the better. On the other hand, the more the bearer of the amulet thinks that it is an incantation that works by a charm-like power, without connection to the mending of his ways, the worse it is, for it causes a person to make his salvation depend on an external thing that is not commanded, instead of making an effort to repent and to purify his soul and his deeds. Still, since some permit it, those who wish to be lenient and accept such an amulet have something to rely on. But an amulet of gentiles, such as an Egyptian scarab, is forbidden to use according to all opinions, because of the prohibition of sorcery (above halakha 7).

sections.title: Desecrating Shabbat in Order to Ask a Tzaddik to Pray for a Sick Person
sections.html:
A question arose among Ḥasidim, who, when they have a dangerously ill person, are accustomed to turn to their righteous Rebbe (tzaddik) to pray for him: is it permitted to desecrate Shabbat for this purpose? In the year 5596 the tzaddik Rabbi Shalom of Belz was a guest in Brody for Shabbat, and on that Shabbat a Jew from among his Ḥasidim in the community of Zolochiv fell dangerously ill, and a halakhic authority (moreh hora'a) permitted desecrating Shabbat by writing a note (kvitel) and sending it, with 'pidyon' money, through a gentile to the Rebbe of Belz. When Rabbi Shlomo Kluger of Brody heard about this, he was greatly incensed and determined that this was an outright desecration of Shabbat.

But those who permitted it argued that the Sages said (Bava Batra 116a): "Whoever has a sick person in his house should go to a sage and he will ask for mercy on his behalf," and since he is dangerously ill, one should desecrate Shabbat in order to rouse the tzaddik to ask for mercy on his behalf. And if one desecrates Shabbat for a segula remedy, all the more so for asking a tzaddik to pray for the dangerously ill person (Degel Maḥane Yehuda). Furthermore, by turning to the tzaddik, the sick person's mind will be settled and he will be strengthened, for he will believe that the tzaddik's prayer will act to save him and restore him to health. And if possible, it is right that the desecrations of Shabbat be done by a gentile, for then the prohibition involved is only rabbinic. And so we learned that when a dangerously ill person asks that his relatives be informed so that they will pray for him and come to hear his will, a gentile messenger is sent on Shabbat to inform them (SA OḤ 306:9; Petaḥ Ha-devir 17).

But those who forbid it brought proof that one does not desecrate Shabbat, even with a rabbinic prohibition, for the sake of prayer, for the Sages said (Ta'anit 14a; 19a) that when situations of danger occur on Shabbat, such as a troop of bandits besieging a city to capture it, or a river whose waters are rising and about to sweep away the houses, or a ship tossed at sea and about to sink, one cries out and prays but does not blow shofars as is customary on fast days, because blowing the shofar on Shabbat is forbidden by rabbinic law (SA 576:13). It follows that one does not desecrate Shabbat even with rabbinic prohibitions for the sake of prayer. This is because one desecrates Shabbat for what human beings do for healing, but for what God will do there is no need to desecrate Shabbat, for God knows that were it not Shabbat they would turn to the tzaddik (the Admor Rabbi Yeḥezkel of Shinova). Furthermore, the merit of keeping Shabbat helps more than prayer. As Rabbi Meir said, one who visits the sick on Shabbat says, "It [Shabbat] can have mercy," and Rashi explained: "If you honour it by not grieving on it."

In practice, according to the overwhelming majority of the poskim, including the Ḥasidic poskim, one may not desecrate Shabbat with Torah prohibitions in order to inform a tzaddik so that he will pray for the sick person. However, they disagreed as to whether it is permitted to ask a gentile to inform the tzaddik, in a way that the prohibition is only rabbinic.9

sections.title: Addressing Angels in Prayer
sections.html:
Some say that one should not say piyyutim (liturgical poems) that contain an address to the angels, such as "You who bring in mercy, bring our [plea for] mercy before the Master of mercy," and "Angels of mercy, servants of the Most High, entreat, please, the face of God with the finest of words," and "Attribute of mercy, roll over us, and cast our supplication before your Maker, and ask mercy on behalf of your people." This is because one should turn in prayer only to God and not to the angels. And so the Sages said (Yerushalmi, Berakhot 9:1) that the Holy One, blessed be He, is not like a king of flesh and blood, to whom one turns through messengers; rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, said: "If trouble comes upon a person, let him cry out neither to Mikhael nor to Gavriel, but let him cry out to Me, and I will answer him immediately." And this is the fifth of the thirteen principles of faith established by the Rambam: "That the Creator, blessed be His name, to Him alone it is fitting to pray, and it is not fitting to pray to anyone besides Him" (above 1:20). And although for many generations Israel was accustomed to say these piyyutim that contain an address to angels, and the piyyut 'Makhnisei Raḥamim' is even mentioned in the order of Seliḥot of Rav Amram Gaon, there were those who ruled not to say them (Responsa Maharam of Rothenburg 270). And some changed the wording so that the request is not directed to the angels but to God, that He instruct the angels who bring up the prayers to bring our prayers up to Him, such as: "May those who bring in mercy bring in our [plea for] mercy" (Maharal, Netiv Ha-avoda 12). And some did not want to abolish the custom so as not to cast aspersions on the earlier generations, but in practice they quietly avoided saying these piyyutim (Ḥatam Sofer 1:166).

On the other hand, most of the rabbis and poskim maintained the custom, and said that it involves no problem of prayer to foreign powers other than God, since it is known to all that the prayers are directed to God, and the request from the angels is that they convey our request and entreaty to Him, may He be blessed, for He gives life to everything and watches over everything. And they mentioned a midrash in which it is said that the Congregation of Israel asks of the angels: "Carry my prayer and my tears before the Holy One, blessed be He, and be advocates of uprightness before Him, that He forgive me for the wilful sins and for the unwitting sins" (Tanya Rabbati 72; Shibbolei Ha-leket).

And in the words of the Sages (Shabbat 12b) we find a sort of source for the idea that one may make use of the help of angels; and therefore they said that one should not pray in Aramaic, because the ministering angels do not understand this language and will not help the prayer to rise. And only where the Shekhina rests, as in a minyan or before a sick person, may one pray in Aramaic, for there is no need for the ministering angels to help the prayer rise (SA OḤ 101:4). Similarly they said (Sanhedrin 44b): "A person should always ask for mercy that all should strengthen his power, and that he should have no adversaries above," and Rashi explained: "that the ministering angels should help him to ask for mercy, and that he should have no accusers above." Indeed, one could argue that the Sages did not say to turn to the angels so that they would ask on our behalf, but only instructed that the prayer be said in a language understood by them, so that they could fulfil their role of bringing up the prayers and would not bring accusations against them. But after all, from the words of the Sages it emerges that the angels help in bringing up prayer, and if so, one may also say piyyutim in which the angels are asked to help bring the prayers up before God.

In summary, it is permitted to say all the piyyutim that Israel has been accustomed to say for generations, even though they contain an address to angels, because it is clear that the prayer itself is directed to God alone. And one who wishes not to say them may refrain, for there is no obligation to say the piyyutim, but he should not protest against those who are accustomed to say them.10
